authors: Albertazzi, U.; Djekic, D.; Ponte Marques, A.
title: Physical climate risk, credit risk and lending activity
question: Causal effect of floods on lending, rates, collateral requirements and default of pre-existing loans
data: AnaCredit loan-level data + Copernicus EMS flood maps; four European floods 2021-2024
identification: Spatial RD at flood boundary (300-500 m); firm-time FE within multi-bank firms
main_finding: Credit +3.5-5% in first quarter then reverses; rates +10-13 bp; default on pre-existing loans +~0.7 pp over two quarters (near doubling); demand dominates; main banks lend ~10 pp more but tighten collateral
how_my_project_differs: Emerging market with thin insurance and debt relief; collateral-level LGD and IFRS 9 staging/ECL rather than firm default only; national-scale 2011 event

authors: Blickle, K. S.; Hamerling, S. N.; Morgan, D. P.
title: How Bad Are Weather Disasters for Banks?
venue: Federal Reserve Bank of New York Staff Reports 990 (Nov 2021, rev. Oct 2025)
question: How much weather disasters hurt bank performance and stability, and why
data: FEMA disasters 1995-2018; SHELDUS county damage; branch-based exposure; FEMA flood maps + HMDA
identification: Panel with saturated FE; non-FEMA vs FEMA disasters and state-border discontinuities for aid
main_finding: Effects small; local banks hit more but a disaster 6.7 SD beyond the 95th percentile would be needed to push a single-county bank to failure; loan demand and local knowledge (avoiding tracts where FEMA maps understate risk) mitigate
how_my_project_differs: Loan/collateral-level rather than bank-level; provisioning and capital via ECL; reverse stress test in a setting without FEMA-style aid or broad insurance

authors: Cortés, K. R.; Strahan, P. E.
title: Tracing out capital flows: How financially integrated banks respond to natural disasters
question: How multi-market banks reallocate credit after local disaster-driven demand shocks
data: HMDA mortgage originations, bank-county-month; US disasters
identification: Property damage instruments lending growth; outcomes in connected unaffected markets; placebo test
main_finding: Small banks cut connected-market credit by a little under 50 cents per extra dollar lent in shocked areas, mainly outside branch markets; more loan sales and higher deposit rates
how_my_project_differs: Studies supply reallocation, not default or loss; US mortgages; my project measures losses on flooded collateral and their capital effect

authors: Koetter, M.; Noth, F.; Rehbein, O.
title: Borrowers under water! Rare disasters, regional banks, and recovery lending
question: Do local banks provide recovery lending and at what cost to stability?
data: 2013 Elbe flood (Germany); ~1.1m firms matched to ~2,000 banks (Creditreform)
identification: Banks in unaffected counties exposed via flooded borrowers vs unexposed banks
main_finding: Exposed banks lend 3% more; connected flooded firms borrow 16% more; no overall risk rise, but exposed banks outside diversified groups show more credit risk and less capital
how_my_project_differs: County-level flood exposure and bank-level risk; no collateral valuation, LGD or ECL; high-income, partly insured setting

title: Flooded Through the Back Door: The Role of Bank Capital in Local Shock Spillovers
venue: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis 57(7):2627-2658
question: Does low bank capital amplify spillovers of a local disaster?
data: Disaster transmitted to firms in non-disaster areas via their banks (event not named in abstract)
identification: Firms connected to strongly exposed low- vs high-capital banks
main_finding: Firms tied to lowest-quartile-capital exposed banks cut borrowing 6.6% and tangible assets 6.9%; banks cut exposure to disaster-prone unaffected areas after a disaster
how_my_project_differs: Capital channel taken as given in my reverse stress test; I measure exposure at collateral level and translate to ECL/CET1

title: Household Finance after a Natural Disaster: The Case of Hurricane Katrina
question: How flooding affects household debt, delinquency and the role of local vs non-local lenders
data: 5% credit-bureau panel matched to Census-block flood depth, New Orleans 2005; HMDA
identification: DiD flooded vs non-flooded blocks using flooding not predicted by engineering risk variables
main_finding: Debt falls via mortgage payoff with flood-insurance proceeds; 90-day delinquency ~10% higher for a year; credit score ~0.06 SD lower for two years; non-local lenders exit
how_my_project_differs: Insurance is the buffer in New Orleans; in Thailand insurance is thin and debt relief dominates, so default and loss channels may differ; I add LGD and bank provisioning

title: Natural disasters and bank stability: Evidence from the U.S. financial system
venue: Journal of Environmental Economics and Management 119:102792
question: Do weather disasters reduce bank stability?
identification: Bank FE and year-region FE; within-bank yearly variation in regional damage
main_finding: Lower Z-scores, higher PD, NPA and foreclosure ratios, lower ROA and equity for two years; recovery after 2-3 years for weather disasters
how_my_project_differs: Bank-level aggregates; I trace losses from flooded collateral through PD/LGD to ECL and capital in an emerging market

authors: Schüwer, U.; Lambert, C.; Noth, F.
title: How Do Banks React to Catastrophic Events? Evidence from Hurricane Katrina
question: How banks in disaster areas respond to Katrina and how banking structure affects recovery
identification: Exogenous hurricane shock; independent vs BHC-affiliated banks
main_finding: Independent highly capitalised banks raise risk-based capital ratios, shift to government securities, cut total loans but increase new lending; counties with such banks grow faster
how_my_project_differs: Bank balance-sheet response only; no collateral or ECL; single US event

title: Access to credit, natural disasters, and relationship lending
question: Effect of aggregate disaster shocks on loan demand and access to credit
data: Client-level data from an Ecuadorian microfinance institution; volcanic eruptions
main_finding: Demand rises but access is restricted; known relationship clients about equally likely to get loans
how_my_project_differs: Emerging-market evidence but microfinance and volcanoes; I study bank collateral, LGD and provisioning for floods

authors: Brei, M.; Mohan, P.; Strobl, E.
title: The impact of natural disasters on the banking sector: Evidence from hurricane strikes in the Caribbean
venue: Quarterly Review of Economics and Finance 72:232-239
question: Impact of hurricane strikes on Caribbean banks
data: Quarterly bank panel, Eastern Caribbean islands; historical hurricane losses
main_finding: Deposit withdrawals cause a funding shock; banks cut lending and draw on liquid assets; no deterioration in defaults or capital
how_my_project_differs: Aggregate bank data in small island economies; I use loan/collateral-level exposure, satellite floods and ECL in a larger EM banking system

title: Financial fragility and natural disasters: An empirical analysis
question: Do large disasters reduce banks' distance-to-default?
main_finding: Disasters raise bank default likelihood, most for geophysical and meteorological events; effect depends on size, supervision and development
how_my_project_differs: Country-level, coarse hazard; I measure within-country, collateral-level exposure

authors: Hosono, K.; Miyakawa, D.; Uchino, T.; Hazama, M.; Ono, A.; Uchida, H.; Uesugi, I.
title: Natural Disasters, Damage to Banks, and Firm Investment
question: Does damage to banks' lending capacity reduce firm investment?
data: Japanese firms and banks around the 1995 Kobe earthquake
identification: Firms outside quake area with main bank inside vs outside
main_finding: Firms whose main bank was in the quake area invested significantly less
how_my_project_differs: Bank-damage supply channel; I focus on borrower collateral damage and bank provisioning

authors: Ivanov, I. T.; Macchiavelli, M.; Santos, J. A. C.
title: Bank lending networks and the propagation of natural disasters
question: How syndicated lending networks propagate disasters
identification: Disaster demand shocks; bank capital heterogeneity; shadow-bank substitution
main_finding: Banks cut credit to distant unaffected regions, more when low-capital; shadow banks offset term loans not credit lines; credit in unaffected regions falls ~3%
how_my_project_differs: Corporate syndicated market in the US; I study collateralised loans and capital adequacy in an EM

authors: Abedifar, P.; Kashizadeh, S. J.; Ongena, S.
title: Flood, Farms and Credit: The Role of Branch Banking in the Era of Climate Change
question: Do local branches provide recovery credit to farmers after a flood?
data: Iran April 2019 flood; proprietary data on 53,000+ farmers
identification: Unexpected flood as natural experiment; relationship strength
main_finding: Branches raise lending for two months, bridging until government aid; stronger-relationship farmers more likely to get recovery loans
how_my_project_differs: Emerging-market flood evidence on credit access, not default, collateral or provisioning

authors: Barbaglia, L.; Fatica, S.; Rho, C.
title: Flooded credit markets: physical climate risk and small business lending
question: Do banks price flood risk in SME loans, and do floods raise SME default?
identification: Flood-risk areas vs others; realised floods
main_finding: 6.4 bp average premium in high-risk areas, larger for longer loans, smaller borrowers and local specialised banks; none for firms with intangible/movable assets; flooded-county firms default more
how_my_project_differs: Pricing and PD in Europe; I add collateral LGD, ECL staging and EM debt relief

authors: Ilabaca, F. E.; Mann, R.; Mulder, P.
title: Global Banks and Natural Disasters
question: How US-regulated global banks adjust cross-border lending after foreign disasters
data: FFIEC 009 country exposures + EM-DAT; quarterly bank-country panel
identification: DiD with country-time FE; heterogeneity by pre-disaster ties
main_finding: Cross-border lending to affected countries falls 9% two years after large disasters, driven by weakly tied banks; interpreted as information frictions
how_my_project_differs: Cross-border flows from US banks; I study domestic bank collateral and provisioning inside an EM
